figures.title: Transformer Model Architecture
figures.caption: The original encoder-decoder Transformer architecture.
explanation: Read the left stack as the encoder: tokens become embeddings, positions are added, then repeated self-attention and feed-forward blocks build contextual representations.
Read the right stack as the decoder: it uses masked self-attention so each generated token cannot look at future target tokens.
The middle connection is encoder-decoder attention: decoder queries attend to encoder outputs so generation can condition on the input sequence.
The repeated Add & Norm boxes are residual connections plus normalization; they stabilize deep stacking and make optimization practical.

figures.title: Scaled Dot-Product and Multi-Head Attention
figures.caption: How attention scores are computed and then repeated across multiple heads.
explanation: Queries ask what information the current token needs; keys advertise what each token can provide; values carry the information that will be mixed.
Scaling before softmax keeps dot products from becoming too large when the key/query dimension grows.
Multi-head attention runs this operation several times in parallel, allowing different heads to specialize in different relationships.

figures.title: Pretraining and Fine-Tuning Flow
figures.caption: BERT first learns general language representations, then adapts the same backbone to downstream tasks.
explanation: The left side shows pretraining: BERT learns from masked words and sentence-pair signals without task-specific labels.
The right side shows fine-tuning: task heads are lightweight, but the full BERT model is updated for the target task.
The same encoder backbone serves classification, question answering, and sentence-pair tasks, which is the main transfer-learning lesson.

figures.title: BERT Input Representation
figures.caption: Token, segment, and position embeddings are summed before entering the Transformer encoder.
explanation: Token embeddings identify the word pieces; position embeddings preserve order; segment embeddings distinguish sentence A from sentence B.
The [CLS] token is placed at the front so its final representation can summarize the sequence for classification.
This diagram is useful when implementing BERT-style inputs because most mistakes come from missing segment or special-token handling.

figures.title: Text-to-Text Framework
figures.caption: T5 casts every NLP task as text input to text output.
explanation: The prefix tells the model what task to perform, such as translation, judgment, acceptability, or summarization.
Labels are generated as text, so classification and generation share the same interface.
This framing anticipates later instruction-tuned systems: tasks become natural-language commands rather than separate model heads.

figures.title: Denoising Objective
figures.caption: Corrupted spans are replaced by sentinel tokens, and the model learns to reconstruct the missing text.
explanation: The input hides spans instead of individual tokens, forcing the model to recover larger chunks of meaning.
Sentinel tokens mark missing regions and organize the target sequence.
This objective teaches both understanding and generation, which fits the encoder-decoder architecture.

figures.title: Zero-Shot, One-Shot, and Few-Shot Prompting
figures.caption: Different ways to ask a language model to perform a task at inference time.
explanation: Zero-shot uses only an instruction, so the model must infer the task from wording alone.
One-shot gives one example, which anchors the desired input-output pattern.
Few-shot gives several examples in the context window; GPT-3's key claim is that larger models use these examples increasingly well without weight updates.

figures.title: Language Model Scaling Laws
figures.caption: Loss improves smoothly as compute, data, and parameter count increase.
explanation: Each plot shows a log-log relationship, which is why the curves look close to straight lines.
The key lesson is predictability: bigger models, more data, and more compute tend to reduce loss in regular patterns.
Use this diagram to understand why later LLM work treats scaling decisions as engineering tradeoffs rather than only model-design choices.

figures.title: Compute-Optimal Model Size
figures.caption: Chinchilla argues that many large models were under-trained relative to their parameter count.
explanation: The diagonal trend compares model size against the compute-optimal frontier.
The central message is that data tokens matter as much as parameter count.
This diagram reframes scaling: for a fixed compute budget, train a smaller model on more tokens instead of only increasing parameters.

figures.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Example
figures.caption: A worked reasoning trace helps the model solve multi-step tasks.
explanation: The standard prompt asks for an answer directly, which can fail on multi-step arithmetic or commonsense reasoning.
The chain-of-thought prompt includes intermediate reasoning before the answer.
For learners, the important point is not the wording alone; it is that examples show the model the desired reasoning format.

figures.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation Overview
figures.caption: A retriever supplies documents that condition the generator.
explanation: The query encoder turns the input into a retrieval query, then the retriever selects relevant documents from an external index.
The generator receives both the original query and retrieved passages, grounding its answer in outside evidence.
RAG-Sequence uses one document set for the whole answer; RAG-Token can vary documents token by token.

figures.title: LoRA Reparameterization
figures.caption: LoRA freezes the original weight matrix and trains two low-rank adapter matrices.
explanation: The large pretrained weight W stays frozen, so the base model does not need to be fully updated.
The trainable update is factored into A and B with rank r, making the number of trainable parameters much smaller.
At inference time, the low-rank update can be merged into the original weight path, avoiding an extra serving penalty in many setups.

figures.title: Training Loss Curves
figures.caption: Training loss decreases smoothly across LLaMA model sizes.
explanation: Each curve corresponds to a model size, showing how loss evolves as more training tokens are consumed.
The larger models generally reach lower loss, but the smooth curve shape also shows stable optimization.
This figure connects LLaMA to scaling-law thinking: quality comes from architecture, data, and training scale together.

figures.title: DPO Compared with RLHF
figures.caption: DPO learns from preference pairs without a separate reward model and RL loop.
explanation: RLHF usually trains a reward model and then optimizes the policy with reinforcement learning.
DPO turns the same preference data into a direct classification-style objective over chosen and rejected responses.
The diagram is the quickest way to see why DPO is simpler operationally: fewer moving parts and no explicit reward-model optimization loop.

figures.title: Reasoning and Acting Prompt Traces
figures.caption: ReAct interleaves thoughts, actions, and observations.
explanation: Standard prompting produces an answer directly; chain-of-thought adds reasoning but may still hallucinate.
Act-only approaches can use tools but lack explicit reasoning traces for planning and correction.
ReAct alternates thought, action, and observation, so the model can use external feedback to revise its next step.

figures.title: Tool-Use Data Generation Pipeline
figures.caption: Toolformer creates its own training examples for API calls.
explanation: The language model proposes possible API calls inside normal text.
The system executes those calls and keeps only examples where the tool result improves prediction.
The final filtered data teaches the model when and how to call tools without requiring a fully hand-labeled tool-use dataset.

figures.title: FlashAttention Tiling
figures.caption: FlashAttention avoids materializing the full attention matrix by tiling computation through fast memory.
explanation: Standard attention writes a large N by N attention matrix to high-bandwidth memory, which becomes a major bottleneck.
FlashAttention tiles Q, K, and V so chunks fit in faster on-chip SRAM.
The important systems idea is IO-awareness: reducing memory traffic can be more important than reducing arithmetic.

figures.title: Mamba Architecture Block
figures.caption: Mamba combines selective state spaces with gating into a simplified sequence block.
explanation: The diagram compares earlier SSM-style blocks with Mamba's simplified block.
Selection lets the model decide which information should enter or affect the recurrent state.
The architecture is designed for long sequences where attention's quadratic cost becomes expensive.

figures.title: Kimi Linear Architecture
figures.caption: Kimi Linear stacks efficient token-mixing blocks that combine linear attention ideas with mixture-style routing.
explanation: The left side shows the repeated model block structure; the right side opens up the token-mixing mechanism.
KDA is the central efficient-attention component, aiming to keep long-context computation practical.
Use this diagram to separate architecture-level choices from the systems claim: lower cache and faster long-context serving.

figures.title: LLM Framework for Education Context
figures.caption: A high-level view of LLM pretraining and fine-tuning in the broader AI stack.
explanation: The nested circles locate LLMs inside deep learning, machine learning, and AI.
The right side separates broad pretraining from task-specific fine-tuning.
For education systems, this helps distinguish general language capability from later adaptation for classroom or tutoring tasks.

figures.title: Taxonomy of LLMs for Education
figures.caption: A taxonomy that groups education applications and representative LLM work.
explanation: Read the left branches as application families, then scan rightward to see representative tasks and systems.
The diagram is useful for project planning because it separates student-facing support, teacher support, and broader educational infrastructure.
Use it as a checklist when asking whether a new education product is tutoring, assessment, content generation, planning, or analytics.

figures.title: Education-Related Foundational Capabilities
figures.caption: A capability map for applying LLMs to educational tasks.
explanation: The left side groups capabilities such as mathematics, writing, programming, and reasoning.
The right side lists representative benchmarks and tasks used to test those capabilities.
For learners, this diagram shows why education LLM evaluation cannot rely on one score; different classroom uses need different abilities.

figures.title: GenMentor System Overview
figures.caption: An LLM-powered multi-agent framework for goal-oriented tutoring.
explanation: The system begins by understanding the learner state and learning goal.
Different agents handle learner modeling, goal adjustment, personalized resources, and content generation.
The diagram is best read as a tutoring workflow: diagnose, plan, generate support, observe feedback, then update the learner model.

figures.title: MWPTutor State Space
figures.caption: A flowchart of tutoring states for guiding math word-problem solving.
explanation: The tutor does not simply answer; it checks alignment, initiates support, pumps for explanation, gives hints, prompts, and escalates when needed.
Decision diamonds represent checks on whether the learner's answer is correct at each step.
This diagram is valuable because it turns vague tutoring behavior into a controllable dialogue policy.

figures.title: Question-Answering vs Thought-Provoking Teaching
figures.caption: A comparison between answer-giving tutoring and Socratic teaching.
explanation: The question-answering pattern gives information directly, which can be efficient but may reduce learner effort.
The thought-provoking pattern asks guided questions so students expose and repair their own reasoning.
Use this diagram to judge whether an AI tutor is teaching the student to think or merely completing the task for them.

figures.title: PlanGlow Planning Interface
figures.caption: The interface combines learner inputs with an explainable study-plan overview.
explanation: The left panel collects constraints such as background, time, subject, and preferred resources.
The right panel turns those constraints into a structured plan that can be inspected and adjusted.
This diagram matters because study planning is not only generation; learners need explanation and control to trust the plan.

figures.title: Classroom Simulacra Framework
figures.caption: A framework for simulating student behavior in online education.
explanation: The framework connects real learning inputs, student history, simulated learning behavior, and simulated outcomes.
Transferable iterative reflection is used to improve how simulated agents respond across contexts.
Read this diagram as a design tool, not a validation guarantee: simulated learners can help explore ideas, but real learner evidence remains necessary.
